title: Sandokai Part 2
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up the second section of the Sandokai, the "Merging of Difference and Unity," drawing on Shohaku Okumura's Living by Vow, Shunryu Suzuki's Branching Streams Flow in the Darkness, and Norman Fischer's talks on the poem. Seishu reads the lines on light and dark, the four elements, and roots and leaves, and borrows Okumura's image of the hand, with five fingers that each have a name and a function yet belong to one body. A 3 a.m. cup of tea, whose warmth, steam, smell, and taste felt unusually vivid, serves as a small example of the relative and the absolute together. Seishu closes by describing the habit of pausing once or twice a day to notice who made the park or the road under the bike, and assigns it as the week's homework.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody and welcome.
Nice to see all of you here.
Last week Tim started on talking about the merging of difference and unity, the chant, the poem, which we occasionally chant here.
What we did as a sangha is divide it up into four different sections, and there will be four of us giving a talk on each section.
So this is section number two that I'm doing tonight.
In preparing for this talk I looked at Shohaku Okumura's book *Living by Vow*.
It's a wonderful book.
He's just an excellent writer, a Japanese priest who's lived in America for probably at least 25 years and writes very clearly about hard things to write about.
In this book *Living by Vow* he goes over the Heart Sutra, the merging of difference and unity, the Bodhisattva vows, and some of the other chants that we do.
The other book I looked at was *Branching Streams Flow in the Darkness* by Shunryu Suzuki.
It's a series of lectures on the merging of difference and unity, I believe done in 1970.
And then by coincidence Norman Fischer gave a series of talks on the Sandokai, which is also called Merging of Difference and Unity, at [unclear: "Lun Lake"] last year.
So I listened to those talks.
The Sandokai, or the merging of difference and unity, refers to both aspects of our lives.
The concrete forms, like human bodies and trees and houses and things like that, and also the absolute: interdependence, emptiness, non-discrimination.
These two sides of life coexist, and this reality is mentioned in many places in Buddhist writing.
In the Heart Sutra: *form does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from form.* The absolute appears in the ordinary and vice versa.
Dogen's writing also comments on this.
I think this quote is also from Shohaku Okumura's book on *Realizing Genjokoan*, which is a book about Dogen's writings.
Here's a quote translated by Shohaku:
*Seeing ultimate reality within concrete phenomena is a basic teaching.
Buddha nature is not something hidden in living beings.
All concrete phenomena and all beings are themselves manifestations of Tathagata or ultimate reality.*
You run into this in many different places.

I don't know if this happens to you, but it often happens to me that when I'm studying something or preparing for a talk, I run into the stuff that I'm writing about or studying in surprising places, not where I'm looking.
Now I didn't find anything in Oprah magazine or *Sports Illustrated*, but I was recently at the YMCA and this quote from Abraham Maslow was posted in the lobby.
He was an American psychologist who lived from 1908 to 1970, and I don't think he was a Buddhist.
Here's what the quote said:
*The great lesson is that the sacred is in the ordinary.
That it is to be found in one's neighbors, friends, and family, in one's backyard.*
That's about as good a summary of what the Sandokai is talking about as anything I could say.
I could just stop my talk right now.
This is what it means, and the story.
But I think I'm supposed to talk for a little longer, so I'll keep going.
The part that I'm going to cover tonight, I'm just going to read you the lines from the poem that I'll be talking about.
This is again the second section:
*Sights vary in quality and form.
Sounds differ as pleasing or harsh.
Refined and common speech come together in the dark.
Clear and murky phrases are distinguished in the light.
The four elements return to their natures just as a child turns to its mother.
Fire heats, wind moves, water wets, earth is solid.
Eye and sights, ear and sounds, nose and smells, tongue and tastes.
Thus with each and everything, depending on these roots, the leaves spread forth.
Trunk and branches share the essence.
Revered and common, each has its speech.*
Throughout the poem, there are examples of the co-occurring existence of the relative and the absolute and how they interact.
In the light, we can see differences and categorize things: big, small, neat, messy, good, bad.
This is discrimination.
In the darkness, everything merges.
Darkness represents the universal aspect of our life, and light is the individual, independent aspect.
In *Living by Vow*, Shohaku Okumura uses the hand as an example of both sides.
Each hand has five fingers.
Each finger has a different function and a different name, but it's also part of a hand and part of a body.
The hand can't operate independently.
The hand can't separate itself from the body.
So we're talking about seeing both sides of life, the independent and the interdependent.
My body is separate from yours.
If I eat, your hunger is not going to be affected.

But my life and all of our lives depend on the sun and the rain and the earth and farmers and people who harvest food and bring it to the market, and the people who build the roads and build the cars, et cetera, et cetera.
Our meditation practice is the same thing.
You can meditate at home by yourself, individually, and in the Zendo you're also kind of meditating by yourself.
But our practice also depends on our ancestors, including the Buddha, all of the ancestors who developed the practice and passed it on to us.
It depends on the people who made these cushions and made the candles and the incense and built this building.
It depends on our teachers and all of us here.
So there's both the individual practice and the together practice, and they coexist.
Now let me look at some of the specific lines.
Differentiation is part of life.
So sights vary, sounds differ, clear and murky phrases can be distinguished.
In the dark, these distinctions disappear, and this is unity.
*The four elements return to their natures just as a child turns to its mother.
Fire heats, wind moves, water wets, earth is solid.* Now these four elements refer to the elements of our lives, to the elements of our body.
Fire represents body heat, wind represents the breath, water represents the blood and tears and other liquids in the body, and earth represents the bones and other solids in the body.
In Buddhism, there's always a fifth element, because these concrete things, whether it's a human body or a lectern or a tree, occupy space.
That's the fifth element, space or emptiness.
The Chinese character for this also means sky.
Every concrete thing occupies space, and that's why the other element is added.
This fits with the view that the relative, in this case the body, and the absolute, space or emptiness, exist together.
Then the next lines: *eye and sights, ear and sounds, nose and smells, tongue and tastes.
Thus with each and everything, depending on these roots, the leaves spread forth.* Here root represents the absolute and leaves the relative.
So day-to-day relative experiences of the senses are rooted in the absolute, which is also Buddha nature.
*Trunk and branches share the essence*, and there's room for both.

*Revered and common, each has its speech.* Over and over again, the Sandokai uses words like dark and light, roots and leaves, trunk and branches, and other things that go together but are different, to point out the coexistence of the relative and the absolute.
I bet all of us have had little glimpses or little experiences of this in our day-to-day lives.
It's not something that just takes place in the mind like an intellectual understanding.
I was trying to think of an example from my life that might be an illustration of this combination of the relative and the absolute.
I'll tell you the story and you can tell me if it fits or not.
A couple years ago, I was having trouble sleeping.
I woke up at two or three in the morning.
I think it was winter time, so it was really dark and really quiet.
I got up and went downstairs, and the house, the neighborhood, was quiet, dark.
I thought, well, I'll make a cup of tea.
So I did what I always do.
I boiled water, I got a cup, I threw a teabag in, poured the water in, let it sit for a while.
Then I thought, well, I'll sit in the living room for a while.
So I picked up the cup and started walking into the living room, and I could really feel the warmth of the tea in the cup, in my hands.
I could see the steam rising from the cup and I could smell the tea.
It smelled really good, very strong, a really nice smell.
I walked to this rocking chair and sat down and took a sip of the tea, and it tasted really good.
I was amazed.
Wow.
I swallowed it and it seemed like I could feel it go all the way into my stomach, and taste it for part of that way, not all the way down.
That doesn't happen to me very often, where I can feel something go all the way into my stomach.
That was the best cup of tea I've ever had in my life.
And it's the tea I make every day.
I haven't had another cup like that since.
But it's the same thing.
To me that seems like a little example of a combination of the relative and the absolute.
I don't know what you think.
I can't explain why it was so good that particular time and why all of those things happened.
But they did.
To finish up, I just want to mention one more side effect, you could say, of doing this talk and preparing this talk.
With the reading and the listening to the talks by Norman, there were just many examples of how interconnected things are.
The examples I gave were of the food that we eat and all the things that it depends on that are outside of us, other people and the weather and nature.
What I found myself doing after a little while is, once or twice a day, whatever I was doing, I would just stop and think about that.
If I was at Boulevard Park, I'd look and think, somebody made this park.
I look at the water and I look at the clouds and I look at the sun, and I didn't do any of that.
Yet I'm really appreciating that and I'm benefiting from that.
Or if I was riding my bike, somebody made the bike and somebody built the road that I was riding on, and that kind of thing.
Just to reflect on how much in my life comes from outside of me, comes from other people or nature, and how wonderful that is, it made me much more grateful.
To do that once or twice a day has been a great practice.

It beats the heck out of making a list of the little things that are pissing me off during the day, or the things that haven't been going the way I want them to, because there's plenty of that as well.
But to just reflect once or twice a day on all that we have that comes from other people, from outside of us, that just enriches our life.
I think that's part of what the Sandokai is talking about too.
So I recommend that practice.
I think Tim gave you a little homework last week, and this will be the homework that I ask you to do this week: to take this time once or twice a day and just reflect on that.
So thank you very much.
